title: Meet N Greet

jokes.text: The Halloween shopping list escalation: 'Blood orphans. No blood orphans. I don't know what that is.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are excitedly listing Halloween party supplies in a talking head, building a rhythm of spooky-but-normal items with April occasionally clarifying 'fake ones'.
jokes.punchline: Andy suggests 'blood orphans' as a party supply, April flatly rejects it, and Andy admits he doesn't even know what it means.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The entire opening sequence is a beautifully constructed escalating rhythm between Andy (chaotic enthusiast) and April (dark but still functioning adult), and 'blood orphans' is the perfect absurdist peak. The joke works on multiple levels: Andy's wordless confidence in suggesting it, April's immediate veto, and then Andy's admission that he made up the phrase without knowing what it meant. It's deeply character-specific — only Andy could deliver this with that particular brand of innocent sincerity. The economy is superb: three lines, maximum comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We could have a bouncy castle, a dunk tank, maybe some face painting...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We could murder someone!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I mean... we could have a murder mystery game! You know, like a fun party game where everyone tries to solve a fake murder.

jokes.text: The 'dead people we just murdered / not murdered, but pictures of dead people from TV or movies' correction
jokes.setup: Andy and April are listing party features in an upbeat talking head, with April occasionally clarifying that violent-sounding things are 'fake ones'.
jokes.punchline: Andy says they'll have 'dead people that we just murdered,' then self-corrects to 'not murdered, but pictures of dead people from TV or movies' — an absurdly specific clarification that raises more questions than it answers.
jokes.explanation: Solid Andy character comedy. The self-correction is the joke — he starts with something alarming, walks it back, but the walkback is still oddly specific and raises new questions. Why pictures of dead people from TV specifically? The phrase 'from TV or movies' is a funny qualifier. Very much in Andy's register of accidentally saying alarming things and then over-explaining.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We could have a piñata, but instead of candy, it's full of hornets.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And instead of a stick, everyone just punches it with their bare fists.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Or we could just set the whole thing on fire and call it a bonfire.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you set the piñata on fire? It's already full of hornets.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Exactly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

jokes.text: 'I hate talking about myself.' / 'Get over it. I talk about myself constantly. Everyone loves me for it.' / 'I really am amazing.'
jokes.setup: Tom is coaching Leslie on campaign messaging, telling her to keep the conversation on herself.
jokes.punchline: Tom's coaching advice is indistinguishable from his own narcissistic worldview, and he immediately proves it by saying 'I really am amazing' — ostensibly about himself, not Leslie.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. The joke is that Tom's advice for Leslie is just a description of how he lives his own life, and 'I really am amazing' as a non-sequitur confirms it. The beat where it's unclear if he's still coaching Leslie or has simply started talking about himself is the sweet spot. Very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Everyone loves me because I talk about myself constantly. It's my best quality.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Like, did you know I have a really good smile? People say it's my best feature.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Also, I'm an excellent listener. I love listening to people talk about me.

jokes.text: The opposition research dossier includes 'prescription medications'
jokes.setup: Leslie presents Tom with a detailed research file on Martin Kernston: 'Photos, bios, likes, dislikes...'
jokes.punchline: The list ends with 'prescription medications' — implying Leslie has somehow obtained private medical records for a meet-and-greet.
jokes.explanation: A neat joke that reveals Leslie's over-preparation has crossed into something ethically questionable, delivered with complete matter-of-factness. The escalation from normal (photos, bios) to invasive (prescription medications) lands cleanly. Economy is excellent — one extra item on a list, maximum implication.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'd like to introduce you to the Duke of Rubber Nipples, sovereign ruler of the Kingdom of Inappropriateness.

jokes.text: Tom claims to know Martin Kernston's advisors; Leslie reveals she made up both names on the spot
jokes.setup: Leslie tests Tom's claimed knowledge of Kernston by asking which advisor he trusts more — 'Ted Flirtman or Rex Baggs?'
jokes.punchline: Tom confidently analyzes the fake advisors. Leslie deadpans: 'I made up both those names.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Leslie's confident questioning sounds authoritative, the names 'Ted Flirtman' and 'Rex Baggs' are funny in themselves (Flirtman especially), Tom's detailed analysis of a fictional person ('Flirtman is more of a confidant') is a great character reveal, and then 'I made up both those names' lands as a devastating, perfectly timed deflation. It reveals character for both: Leslie's shrewd preparation vs. Tom's bluffing. The joke is also deeply earned — it pays off Tom's bragging while establishing Leslie's competence. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, Leslie, I'm gonna test your knowledge of Kernston's advisors. Who was Kernston's trade minister in 1987?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Um... Gerald Hutchins?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wrong. It was actually... I have no idea. I made up this entire test. Kernston isn't even a real place.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I just wanted to see how long you'd pretend to know about something you didn't actually know about.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio calling Tom in tears (inferred from 'Jean-Ralphio, stop crying')
jokes.setup: Tom is in the middle of the meet-and-greet prep when his phone rings.
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate response — 'Jean-Ralphio, stop crying. What? Hold on. Slow down.' — implies Jean-Ralphio (a grown man) is calling in hysterics, a hilarious character detail.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that rewards fans of Jean-Ralphio. The comedy is entirely in what we infer — a flamboyant, over-the-top character crying on the phone — and Tom's weary familiarity with it. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I look like a sumo wrestler that got deflated.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Which is weird because normally you'd think a deflated sumo wrestler would be skinnier, not... worse.

jokes.text: 'I'm a sumo wrestler after he lost the weight.'
jokes.setup: Ben finds the apartment transformed for a Halloween party. Andy is in a sumo suit that appears to not fit properly.
jokes.punchline: Andy's explanation of his costume — a sumo wrestler who has already lost the weight — is a gloriously absurdist concept delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: A standout joke. The concept is brilliantly original — a sumo wrestler post-weight-loss is a genuinely novel costume idea that requires a certain kind of brain to arrive at. The economy is perfect: one sentence explains everything. It's deeply Andy-coded (he's wearing a costume that doesn't really work but he's fully committed to the bit and proud of it). The absurdist logic holds together perfectly. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — a sharp, unexpected, highly quotable joke with perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My family never argued. We just... didn't talk about problems.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My dad left when I was seven and we all just pretended he was at work for ten years.

jokes.text: Ben's passive-aggressive response to not being told about the party: 'I didn't tell you I was gonna be quietly working in my room. That's a good point. Yeah, yeah. I guess we're even.'
jokes.setup: Ben discovers there's an enormous Halloween party happening in his home without anyone telling him.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately concedes the point when Andy says he didn't tell them he'd be working quietly — the logic is absurd, but Ben's WASP-ish conflict-aversion causes him to accept it.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. Ben's capitulation to obviously bad logic is a precise character beat — he's conflict-averse and intellectually honest to a fault, so he genuinely processes Andy's non-argument and accepts it. The 'That's a good point' from Ben is the funniest part. Sets up the episode's Ben/Andy/April subplot cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, why is your face on all these rugs?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because it's one of my life goals to have my face on a rug. I've achieved it.

jokes.text: Ben's exit line: 'If you need me, I'll definitely be awake, because I won't be able to sleep because of the party.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just agreed that he and Andy/April are 'even' for not telling each other things. He's trying to be gracious about the party.
jokes.punchline: His offer to be available is undercut by the reality that he'll be up anyway because of the loud party — delivered as if he's doing them a favor.
jokes.explanation: A solid passive-aggressive exit line. Ben trying to frame his helplessness as generosity is funny and character-specific. The 'So...' trailing off at the end implies the camera lingering on him awkwardly, adding a visual/reaction beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Donna, what are you dressed as?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm a detective.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: How can you tell?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because I'm extremely observant.

jokes.text: Ben's confessional about his family: 'My parents' method of problem solving is to keep everything bottled up and subtly hint at what's bothering them. And after 36 years, they are still divorced.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains his family's non-confrontational approach to conflict resolution, building expectation that this strategy at least keeps the family together.
jokes.punchline: 'And after 36 years, they are still divorced.' — the method didn't work, AND they've maintained the failed relationship dynamic even post-divorce for 36 years.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect talking-head joke. The setup is classically structured — you expect 'and after 36 years, they have a great marriage' or similar. 'Still divorced' is the first twist, but the real joke is 'still' — implying that being divorced is a continuous active state they've maintained for 36 years while also keeping up the same dysfunctional communication patterns. It's dark, character-illuminating (explains so much about Ben), and perfectly economical. The double meaning of 'still' (continuing to be / as in, even now) is elegant wordplay. Earns its 8.0.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Sherlock Holmes is the greatest character ever created. A man of unparalleled intellect and deductive reasoning.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: But honestly, I think I'm a more well-rounded version of him. I have his analytical mind, but I also have emotional intelligence and the ability to connect with people on a human level.

jokes.text: Tom's party decorations for Leslie's meet-and-greet look like an Entertainment 720 promotional event, with Tom's face on rugs
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the venue expecting a tasteful small-business meet-and-greet she asked Tom to organize.
jokes.punchline: The decorations are extravagant and feature Tom's face on rugs — Tom has turned Leslie's campaign event into an Entertainment 720 promotion.
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy that is entirely character-specific — only Tom would make a campaign event about himself. The rugs with his face are a lovely absurd detail. The comedy is in the gap between Leslie's expectations and reality.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Chris, you're texting without looking at your phone.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know. I'm very polite. I make eye contact with people when I talk to them. So I've developed the ability to text without looking.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, it is. I'm living proof.

jokes.text: 'It's always been a dream of mine to be a rug, and it's finally happened.'
jokes.setup: Leslie demands the rugs with Tom's face be removed. Tom is supposed to be contrite.
jokes.punchline: Instead of apologizing, Tom is DELIGHTED that his face is on rugs, framing it as a childhood dream fulfilled.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom Haverford joke. 'It's always been a dream of mine to be a rug' is a brilliantly specific and original statement — who has this dream? Only Tom. The delivery almost certainly includes sincere nostalgia, which makes it funnier. It's a perfect capsule of his character: grandiose, self-absorbed, and completely earnest about it. High quotability — the kind of line fans repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Andy, there's a live wire hanging directly above the bathtub.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I call that the Shock Tub 3000.

jokes.text: Donna in police costume: 'You are a policewoman.' / 'Yep. You're a regular Sherlock Holmes. I solved that mystery before you did.'
jokes.setup: Chris (dressed as Sherlock Holmes) observes Donna's costume and states the obvious.
jokes.punchline: Donna fires back that she figured out her own costume before he did, using his Sherlock Holmes identity against him — she's quicker at deduction than the world's greatest detective.
jokes.explanation: A sharp comeback with clean structure. The setup (Chris dressed as Sherlock stating the obvious) creates the perfect irony for Donna's retort. The logic is airtight — of course she solved the mystery of her own costume first — and delivered with Donna's characteristic bluntness. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is all this? I expected tools, not... is this a unicorn plushie?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's a mood ring unicorn, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And what's this? A bottle of nail polish labeled 'Sunset Dreams'?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's for when we need a manicure break during woodworking.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A tiara. There's a tiara in here.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: For formal tool use.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And finally, a flashlight filled with... candy?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So you can see AND snack in the dark, Ron.

jokes.text: Ron's Sherlock Holmes confessional: 'Sherlock Holmes is literally the greatest character in the Western canon... Replace his pasty British frailty with superhuman physical fitness, and you get... Sherlock Traeger.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains his admiration for Sherlock Holmes in a talking head, building a seemingly sincere literary appreciation.
jokes.punchline: The 'improvement' Ron has identified is replacing Holmes's intellect-first physicality with 'superhuman physical fitness' — essentially making Holmes into Ron — and naming the result 'Sherlock Traeger' (Traeger being a brand of wood-fired grill, beloved by Ron).
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the series' finest Ron Swanson moments. The structure is immaculate: Ron begins with genuine-sounding literary appreciation ('the greatest character in the Western canon'), escalates with specific critique ('pasty British frailty' is a perfect phrase), proposes his enhancement (superhuman physical fitness — i.e., Ron himself), and then lands 'Sherlock Traeger' — a portmanteau that sneaks in Ron's beloved grill brand. Every word earns its place. It's only achievable with this specific character. The pomposity, the self-insert, the grill reference — this is the Platonic ideal of a Ron Swanson joke. Scores comparably to the 9.5 anchor example in craft, though slightly lower impact as it's not quite the cultural touchstone that the vasectomy line became.

dialogue.speaker: Business Owner
dialogue.line: You've never bought a salad from us.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's true. I don't eat salad. I think salad is what food eats.

jokes.text: Jerry dressed as Mr. Potato Head — confirmed by 'That's right' with no elaboration
jokes.setup: Andy is announcing costumes. 'Mr. Potato Head.'
jokes.punchline: Jerry confirms he is indeed Mr. Potato Head with a simple 'That's right' — a costume presumably as unglamorous and earnest as Jerry himself.
jokes.explanation: Functional visual gag. Mr. Potato Head is a perfect Jerry costume — a lovable, silly, slightly pathetic character. It doesn't transcend the basic joke but it's well-matched to the character's running gag of being the butt of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mr. Kernston, I'd like to present my new business concept: 'Rent-tainment.' It's like rent, but it's also entertainment.

dialogue.speaker: Martin Kernston
dialogue.line: That's just rent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Rent-tainment. The 'tainment' is silent.

jokes.text: Chris (Sherlock Holmes) asking about April: 'Where's my lovely daughter tonight?' — then explaining he was worried Ben might be worried seeing them together
jokes.setup: Chris, dressed as Sherlock Holmes at a Halloween party, brings up his daughter to Ben (her boyfriend).
jokes.punchline: Chris proactively addresses a concern Ben didn't raise — that Ben might be uncomfortable seeing Chris and his daughter together — which is itself socially awkward, and Chris's relentless positivity makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Competent cringe comedy rooted in Chris's oblivious over-positivity. The setup of addressing a concern that wasn't raised is a good structure, but it doesn't fully land — the joke is slightly underpowered.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need to be very careful about my language. I can't just go around calling people 'butt-head' willy-nilly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's why I have a carefully curated list of insults I use only in the most extreme circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Like... buttface, turd-guzzling thunder-cunt, and worse.

jokes.text: Chris texting without looking at his phone to maintain eye contact: 'I think it's rude not to maintain eye contact with the people that I'm talking to.'
jokes.setup: Ben is surprised Chris can text without looking at his phone.
jokes.punchline: Chris has developed an absurd skill specifically to enforce his extreme social politeness, framing it as an ethical position.
jokes.explanation: Very good Chris Traeger joke. His extreme pursuit of positive social behavior has led him to develop an unusual physical skill, and he frames it as an ethical obligation. It's original (most Chris jokes are about health/positivity, not skill development), has perfect character integration, and the visual of him confidently texting while maintaining unbroken eye contact is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Jerry, I need your help with a home repair project.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, Ron, I'd be happy to help! By the way, it's not a costume, it's my outfit.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't care what you call it, Gerry. Now hand me that wrench.

jokes.text: Ben's high-five reaction to Chris's texting feat — 'Wow! That's amazing!' followed by 'Wow.'
jokes.setup: Chris demonstrates blind texting. Ben is genuinely impressed.
jokes.punchline: Ben gives a sincere, enthusiastic high-five and two rounds of 'Wow' — he's been completely won over by a trivial party trick despite his current low-level feud with April and Andy.
jokes.explanation: A light reaction beat. Ben's earnestness breaking through his mild annoyance is consistent with his character, and 'Wow.' twice is a small funny beat. Not a strong joke but contributes to the scene's rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's not doing it. He said it was 'undignified.' Which is hilarious, because Ben once spent an entire meeting with the state comptroller with a Cheeto stuck to his forehead.

jokes.text: Ron noticing the leaky faucet while dressed as a pirate at Andy and April's Halloween party
jokes.setup: Ron arrives at the party in the same pirate costume he apparently wore last year ('Weren't you a pirate last year?'), then immediately pivots to home maintenance.
jokes.punchline: 'Yes. This is my Halloween costume.' Ron refuses to engage with the implication that he should have a new costume, and immediately pivots to noticing a maintenance problem — Ron at a party is still Ron.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron joke. The pirate callback (same costume every year) is character-perfect — Ron finds something that works and does not deviate from it. His dismissal of the implied criticism ('Yes. This is my Halloween costume.') is a masterpiece of deadpan. And then immediately noticing the leaky faucet while in pirate costume is the perfect character summary: Ron Swanson will always notice infrastructure problems and will always address them, regardless of context.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Come on, Ben. Just tell me how you really feel.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I feel... adequate.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Adequate? That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My heart rate is normal. I have consumed sufficient calories. These are positive indicators.

jokes.text: 'I just stuffed a sock in it yesterday. What else do they want me to do?'
jokes.setup: Ron informs Andy that his bathroom faucet is leaking.
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals his DIY solution was to stuff a sock in the faucet, and then acts genuinely put-upon that this hasn't been sufficient.
jokes.explanation: Strong Andy joke. The sock solution is perfectly Andy-brained — a child's approach to a serious problem. But the real kicker is 'What else do they want me to do?' — his genuine exasperation at the faucet's ingratitude. He treated a leak with a sock yesterday, what more could be required? Deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We've got Jerry's Fried Dough, Sweetums, and the Mobile Phone Emporium all here tonight!

jokes.text: 'Shock wire. I call it that, 'cause if you take a shower, and you touch the wire, you die!'
jokes.setup: Ron has now found an exposed wire above Andy's bathtub.
jokes.punchline: Andy has named the wire himself, demonstrating full awareness that it causes death, but treating it as a fun piece of home trivia rather than an emergency.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Shock wire' as a casual household term Andy invented is brilliantly funny. The explanation ('because if you take a shower, and you touch the wire, you die') has perfect structure — the pause before 'you die' and the exclamation point in the transcript suggest it's delivered with perverse pride. And Ron's flat 'Yes, that is accurate' confirming the murder hazard as if it's a reasonable assessment makes it even better. Andy has identified a death hazard, named it, and considers the situation adequately addressed. This is dark, brilliant, and completely in character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, if you hijack this event, I will hurt you in a way that only Ben Wyatt could describe using his forensic accounting skills.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to make your finances so complicated that even the IRS won't understand them.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional revealing April and Andy's 'toolbox': a hammer, half a pretzel, baseball card, a 'Sonic and Hedgehog' cartridge, a scissor half, and a flashlight filled with jelly beans
jokes.setup: Ron asks if they have a toolbox. Andy says yes. Ron presents it to the camera in a talking head.
jokes.punchline: The 'toolbox' is an absurdist collection of random objects culminating in 'a flashlight filled with jelly beans' — none of which is a real tool. The Sonic cartridge being listed as 'Sonic and Hedgehog' (not Sonic the Hedgehog) is a bonus detail.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. The escalating list of non-tools is perfectly constructed — each item is worse than the last, culminating in 'a flashlight filled with jelly beans,' which is such a specific and demented detail that it earns a huge laugh. The 'Sonic and Hedgehog' misnaming is a beautiful bonus (either Andy doesn't know the correct title or Ron is reading it off the label phonetically). Ron presenting this to the camera with the gravity of a crime scene investigator is the perfect delivery context. This is the kind of joke that gets clipped and shared.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I fixed the shelf. I actually fixed it. Do you understand what this means? I'm a man now. A real man. I can build things. I can provide. I could survive in the wilderness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You used a level and some screws.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I am a god.

jokes.text: Leslie tells the crowd she's personally patronized every business; a woman challenges her on Sue's Salads. Leslie: 'That's because I don't hate myself, Tania.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to charm business owners by claiming to patronize all their establishments. A salad shop owner calls her bluff.
jokes.punchline: Leslie abandons the diplomatic pretense entirely and directly insults salad — and the woman — with 'That's because I don't hate myself, Tania.'
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Leslie Knope joke. She's in full campaign-professional mode trying to win votes, gets caught in a lie by a salad shop owner, and her response is to insult salad and the business owner directly. The pivot from 'chasing your vote' (acknowledging the political reality) to 'I stand behind my decision to avoid salad and other disgusting things' is perfectly Leslie — she cannot pretend to like something she finds disgusting, even for political gain. 'That's because I don't hate myself, Tania' is highly quotable and specific. The use of her name ('Tania') adds a wonderful personal touch.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Entertainment 720 is the best company ever. We invented Facebook.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'When in doubt, in Pawnee, slam salad.'
jokes.setup: After insulting the salad shop owner at what was supposed to be a business-friendly event, Leslie gives a talking-head assessment.
jokes.punchline: She has derived a political lesson from her gaffe that entirely validates her bad behavior — 'when in doubt, slam salad' — as if this is a legitimate campaign strategy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie confessional. She's taken a campaign blunder and reframed it as a strategic insight. 'Slam salad' as a political tactic is a great phrase. The joke reveals the self-serving nature of Leslie's optimism — she can rationalize any mistake into a win. Economy is superb.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My brother and I have a very normal sibling relationship. We fight, we make up, we set each other's stuff on fire. You know, typical brother and sister stuff.

jokes.text: Leslie about the Harvest Festival: 'No. Yes. Well, it was a team effort. I barely did anything. I held them back, actually. They succeeded despite me.'
jokes.setup: Martin Kernston asks if Leslie was responsible for the Harvest Festival, clearly as a compliment.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's bureaucratic self-effacement immediately overrides her instinct to take credit, and she escalates to actively claiming she sabotaged the event — she undersells herself so hard she accidentally insults herself.
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. The 'No. Yes.' opening is great — Leslie's instincts fighting each other. But the escalation to 'They succeeded despite me' is the payoff, and it's funny because it's so clearly untrue and Leslie is clearly cringing as she says it. Her professional modesty runs so deep it becomes self-destructive.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My family has this thing where we fight, then we make up, then we fight again. It's like a cycle.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My dad would punch my uncle, then they'd go get a beer together, then next Thanksgiving my uncle would punch my dad back.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's beautiful, really. Very balanced.

jokes.text: Tom says the Harvest Festival 'launched Entertainment 720'; Leslie says 'No one says that'; Tom: 'I just said it.'
jokes.setup: Tom claims the Harvest Festival 'launched' Entertainment 720 as a credibility boost
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'No one says that' is immediately countered by Tom's perfectly logical 'I just said it' — technically true, utterly useless
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. 'I just said it' is three words that perfectly expose Tom's logical sleight of hand. Classic setup/punchline with maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, everything is fine. My company is doing great. We're expanding, we're profitable, we're—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, your office is literally a closet.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a small space, that's part of our brand. We're lean, we're efficient—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your website just says 'Tom's Company' and then it's a 404 error.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, well, we're still in beta. The company has completely failed.

jokes.text: 'I don't like to throw around the word butt-head too often... But I can say without hesitation that Tom is being a real dick.'
jokes.setup: Leslie begins what sounds like a measured, diplomatic talking-head about not wanting to overuse insults.
jokes.punchline: The word she reserves for special occasions is 'butt-head,' but then she immediately escalates past it to a much stronger insult — 'a real dick' — without hesitation.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Leslie Knope joke. The structure is immaculate: Leslie sets up a diplomatic framework around not overusing 'butt-head' (already funny — 'butt-head' as the word she treasures), creating expectation that she'll use it carefully. The subversion is that she immediately jumps past it to a stronger, cruder insult, completely abandoning her stated restraint. 'Butt-head' is also perfect Leslie vocabulary — it's a PG-13 insult that reveals her character even as she escalates past it. High quotability, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What happened to the company?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, it dissolved. But look at my skin right now — I'm like a soft, buttery biscuit.

jokes.text: Leslie confronting Tom after he monopolized Kernston: 'Why don't you go over to one of your rugs and sit on your own face?'
jokes.setup: Tom has stolen Kernston from Leslie for his own business pitch, and Leslie is furious.
jokes.punchline: Her insult incorporates the rug-with-Tom's-face detail from earlier — she directs him to literally sit on his own face.
jokes.explanation: A highly satisfying callback insult. 'Sit on your own face' is a great phrase that only makes sense in this specific context — the show has set up the rugs earlier precisely so this payoff lands. It's also a perfect expression of Leslie's fury — specific, creative, and biting without being generic. Strong callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My nose is broken! There's blood everywhere!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh no, Andy, we need to get you to a hospital!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is so serious. Everyone, we need to help Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, it's fake blood. I was just messing with you guys.

jokes.text: 'You stole the Nipple King. Thanks a lot, traitor.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been monopolizing Martin Kernston (president of Kernston Rubber Nipples) at Leslie's event
jokes.punchline: Leslie calling him 'the Nipple King' with complete seriousness and moral indignation — as if this is a coveted title worth fighting over
jokes.explanation: 'The Nipple King' being used as a legitimate honorific with genuine gravitas is the joke. The title was established earlier and the payoff here is Leslie deploying it in anger — which makes it funnier than the initial setup.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You've gotta spend money to make money, Leslie. It's just good business sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, that's not a business strategy, that's just... math. And also the reason your last three ventures failed.

jokes.text: Ron approaches April and Andy's house project, calls the beanbag (eggplant): 'You, bean bag, come with me.' / 'I'm an eggplant.' / 'I don't care. Come with me.' / 'Why?' / 'I need small hands.' / 'I'm scared.'
jokes.setup: Ron has decided to fix the house as a wedding gift and has identified April as a useful assistant.
jokes.punchline: Ron calls April 'bean bag' (she's in a vegetable costume), dismisses her correction, gives a cryptic reason ('I need small hands'), and April's response 'I'm scared' is both deadpan and accurate.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful small exchange. Ron's complete indifference to April's costume correction ('I don't care') followed by the mysterious and alarming 'I need small hands' is great Ron Swanson material. 'I'm scared' from April — who is rarely scared of anything — is the cherry on top. The interaction is also sweet in context: Ron is doing this out of affection.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I just have a few reasonable roommate requests. No loud music after 10 PM, please clean up after yourself, and we should probably establish a chore schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. I hear you. But here's my counter-offer: I get to have a pet ocelot, I eat whatever I want from the fridge without asking, and on Thursdays I get to invite the entire Parks Department over to watch me practice my DJ skills until 4 AM.

jokes.text: Ben arriving at the party in no costume: 'He's going as lame.'
jokes.setup: Andy greets Ben's arrival enthusiastically. April notes Ben has no costume.
jokes.punchline: April's assessment — 'He's going as lame' — is delivered flatly and perfectly.
jokes.explanation: A tight April insult with good economy. 'He's going as lame' is exactly April's register — deadpan, contemptuous, and technically observational. It's a standard 'person came without costume' joke elevated by April's delivery style and the context of her ongoing feud with Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: In 1975, we had Watergate, we had Vietnam, and we had to say goodbye to David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona.

jokes.text: Andy suggesting Ben wear the Batman costume: 'I think the Batman costume is way better. You should go wear that.' / Ben: 'Yeah, I don't think I'm gonna put on a costume, because I'm not really attending this party that's at my house.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to get Ben to dress up, suggesting Batman.
jokes.punchline: Ben's response reframes his presence at his own party as non-attendance — a perfectly logical but emotionally passive-aggressive position.
jokes.explanation: A good Ben moment. 'I'm not really attending this party that's at my house' is a beautifully specific piece of passive-aggressive reasoning. He's technically present but refuses to acknowledge attendance. Very Ben — his conflict-aversion manifests as denial of reality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom is a lot of things. He's lazy, he's vain, he's a terrible friend.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But what Tom is, above all else, is a tiny little person. And I mean that with all the love in my heart.

jokes.text: Ben attempts to express his feelings, gets flustered: 'My name's Ben. I'm mad.'
jokes.setup: Andy tells Ben to talk about what's bothering him. Ben initially denies being mad, then Andy persists.
jokes.punchline: Ben's attempt to demonstrate anger results in a bizarrely formal self-introduction: 'My name's Ben. I'm mad.' — as if he's at an anger management meeting.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ben joke. The abrupt, formal self-introduction mid-emotional-moment is perfectly timed and deeply character-specific. Ben is so repressed and conflict-averse that his attempt to express anger comes out as a support-group introduction. 'My name's Ben. I'm mad.' is extremely quotable. Economy score nearly perfect — five words that say everything about the character.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Jerry, I want to be completely transparent with you. I'm seeing your daughter, and I think it's important you know that our physical relationship is very—

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Chris, please, I'm begging you. I do not need to know this. I really, really don't.

jokes.text: The Orin-at-the-door visual/reaction beat: 'Orin, no! No! Stay out!'
jokes.setup: There's a soft kissing moment (presumably between Andy and April), then someone tries to enter.
jokes.punchline: April yells at Orin — her creepy friend — to stay out. The implication that Orin has materialized at an inopportune moment and is being turned away is a great unseen character joke.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. Orin appearing in inappropriate moments is an established running gag, and 'No! Stay out!' has good energy. Not a strong joke on its own but rewards fans of the character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh wow, a detective. So where are your keys?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because I've been watching you pat down your pockets for twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Leslie's speech listing local businesses including 'Glennmore Discount Cemetery,' 'Tramp Stamp Tattoos,' 'Enormous Kenny's Fried Dough Stand and Mobile Phone Emporium,' 'Smooth Operator Bikini Waxes'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving a heartfelt speech to local small business owners, listing them by name.
jokes.punchline: The businesses of Pawnee are a parade of hilariously specific and inappropriate establishments — a discount cemetery, tattoo parlor, enormous fried dough stand that also sells phones, bikini wax place — all listed with the same civic pride as a normal town's businesses.
jokes.explanation: Parks and Rec world-building comedy at its best. The business names are lovingly crafted — 'Glennmore Discount Cemetery' (discount! for death!) and 'Enormous Kenny's Fried Dough Stand and Mobile Phone Emporium' (the juxtaposition of fried dough and phone retail is perfect) are standouts. This is the show doing what it does best: treating Pawnee as a specific, weird place with internal logic.

jokes.text: Tom hijacking Leslie's speech to promote Entertainment 720
jokes.setup: Leslie has given Tom credit in her speech ('And Entertainment 720'). Tom takes the microphone.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately pivots to pitching his own company, complete with a jingle ('Entertainment 720 / Where dreams come, they come true'), entirely derailing the campaign event.
jokes.explanation: Strong character moment. Tom's complete inability to resist self-promotion, even in a context where it actively harms his best friend's campaign, is on-brand. The jingle ('Where dreams come, they come true' — grammatically broken) is a nice absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Leslie to Tom after the promotional video: 'You're lucky that Martin Kernston is here, 'cause you're gonna need another nipple. Why?'
jokes.setup: Tom has played an embarrassing promotional video that's derailing Leslie's event. She threatens him.
jokes.punchline: The threat references Kernston's business ('Kernston Rubber Nipples') — she's going to do something to Tom requiring an extra nipple. Tom's confused 'Why?' suggests he doesn't even understand his own potential fate.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that incorporates Kernston's business name into a threat. The threat itself is deliberately vague and weird (you'll need an extra nipple), which is funnier than a specific threat. Tom's 'Why?' is a perfect button — he's so self-absorbed he doesn't even process the implied violence.

jokes.text: Ron and April fixing the faucet: Ron's obvious pride and satisfaction in completing the repair, culminating in 'Damn it, I just love it so much.'
jokes.setup: Ron has fixed the leaky faucet. He and April are experiencing genuine satisfaction.
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it, I just love it so much' — Ron's emotional response to home repair is more effusive than his emotional response to almost anything interpersonal.
jokes.explanation: Lovely Ron character moment. The 'Damn it' framing a positive emotion is perfect Ron — he's almost annoyed at himself for feeling so much. His love of craft and functionality running deeper than social emotions is a well-established character trait, and 'I just love it so much' about fixing a faucet is funny precisely because of what it's not being said about.

jokes.text: The fake Mark Zuckerberg character in Tom's promotional video: 'I can't reveal my identity because of various corporate enemies... I invented Facebook.'
jokes.setup: Tom shows a promotional video featuring a testimonial from someone claiming to be a social media mogul.
jokes.punchline: After a long preamble about keeping his identity secret, the man immediately says 'I invented Facebook' — completely undermining his own anonymity.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed absurdist joke. The structure of elaborate secrecy immediately followed by self-revelation is classic. Tom hired someone to impersonate Mark Zuckerberg for his promotional video, but the actor doesn't understand subtlety. The detail that this person calls himself 'fairly popular social networking site' before the reveal adds a layer.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I know that video seemed like the rantings of a lunatic pretending to be Mark Zuckerberg.' / Tom: 'That's who that was?' / Leslie: 'No.'
jokes.setup: After the video, Leslie tries to do damage control with Kernston.
jokes.punchline: Tom's question ('That's who that was?') reveals he didn't even know who his own promotional actor was impersonating, and Leslie's flat 'No' is both a denial and an acknowledgment of the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Excellent three-line exchange. Leslie's characterization of the video as 'rantings of a lunatic' is already good, but Tom's genuine 'That's who that was?' reveals he made a fake Zuckerberg video without knowing who Zuckerberg was, and Leslie's 'No' — technically a denial but functionally an acceptance of the chaos — lands perfectly. Clean, economical, character-specific.

jokes.text: The E 720 Mailing List Divas performance: dancers asking business owners to write down their direct contact info for whoever handles hiring
jokes.setup: Tom introduces 'the E 720 Mailing List Divas' as entertainment at a business meet-and-greet.
jokes.punchline: The 'divas' are apparently dancers who incorporate a direct sales pitch — asking for hiring contact info while performing — into their routine. Tom has turned client acquisition into performance art.
jokes.explanation: A good absurdist visual — dancers performing while simultaneously collecting business leads. It's Tom's grandiosity applied to something as mundane as a mailing list. The specific detail of 'write down the name and direct phone line for whoever is in charge of hiring independent contractors' during a dance is funny.

jokes.text: Tom announces an 'E 720 Mobile Hot Tub' parked outside
jokes.setup: Tom's promotional event keeps escalating in absurdity.
jokes.punchline: He has brought a mobile hot tub — on a vehicle — to a business networking event.
jokes.explanation: A solid absurdist escalation. A mobile hot tub is a very Tom Haverford concept — unnecessary luxury combined with logistical complexity. Sets up the later payoff where Tom and Leslie are having their emotional conversation while sitting in it.

jokes.text: Leslie denying Ben the Halloween candy: 'If you're not part of the party, you can't have the candy. Back up.'
jokes.setup: Ben is eating a Butterfinger, ostensibly not at the party. April confronts him.
jokes.punchline: April enforces party membership rules with the gravity of a bouncer — 'Back up' — and Ben actually backs up. Her authority over her own home is total.
jokes.explanation: Good April/Ben character comedy. April treating Ben as an uninvited guest in his own home is a perfectly absurd power dynamic, and 'Back up' delivered with total authority is funny. Ben's compliance is the real joke.

jokes.text: April's confessional about her sister: 'We steal each other's stuff, hack each other's Twitter accounts, set each other's clothes on fire. There are no rules.'
jokes.setup: April explains her approach to sibling conflict, framing it as normal sister behavior.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'steal each other's stuff' (normal) to 'hack Twitter accounts' (modern but plausible) to 'set each other's clothes on fire' (arson) is delivered as if these are equivalent behaviors. 'There are no rules' is the dark cherry on top.
jokes.explanation: Excellent April character joke. The escalation is perfectly paced — each item is more severe, culminating in actual arson, and 'There are no rules' endorses all of it equally. This reveals April's genuine nihilism and also contextualizes her willingness to physically fight Ben. Deeply character-specific and very quotable.

jokes.text: April physically dragging Ben into his room to force him to express his feelings: 'I'm going to beat you up until you do, because I'm mature.'
jokes.setup: April wants Ben to express what's bothering him. He resists talking.
jokes.punchline: April's solution to Ben's emotional repression is to physically force it out of him — and she justifies it by claiming maturity.
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. 'I'm going to beat you up until you do, because I'm mature' is a perfectly April statement — inverting adult logic (mature people talk things out) to justify violent behavior. The self-awareness of calling it mature while describing assault is funny.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional about the Dwyer method: 'yelling, wrestling, crying, followed by lots of hugs, then more wrestling, but the fun kind, then crying when the fun kind of wrestling got out of hand.'
jokes.setup: Andy explains his family's conflict resolution method as an alternative to Ben's passive-aggressive approach.
jokes.punchline: The Dwyer method escalates from yelling to wrestling to crying to hugs to more wrestling (fun) to crying again (when fun wrestling got out of hand) — a perfectly circular, childlike approach to conflict.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Andy joke. The Dwyer method is a beautifully designed piece of character comedy — it describes a chaotic, childlike family and the joke is in the precise taxonomy Andy assigns to it. The escalation structure is perfect: the 'fun kind' distinction for wrestling, and then the third crying being caused by the fun wrestling getting out of hand, creates a complete and absurd loop. It couldn't be delivered by anyone but Andy. Very quotable, very high rewatch value.

jokes.text: Leslie finding Tom hiding in the mobile hot tub: 'Get out of there right now... or we are no longer friends. I'm not getting out. Fine. Then I'm getting in.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has had enough of Tom. She finds him hiding in his mobile hot tub.
jokes.punchline: When her ultimatum fails, Leslie's solution is to GET IN the hot tub — abandoning any pretense of dignity to confront him at his level, in his medium.
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic escalation and callback. Leslie's decision to climb into the hot tub in what is presumably her work clothes (or possibly still event attire) rather than back down is both funny and deeply Leslie — she will not be denied a confrontation. The visual of two people arguing in a hot tub while one is fully clothed is great physical comedy.

jokes.text: 'Well, maybe we should get out of this hot tub.' / 'I'm too sad to get out, and I'm all pruney.'
jokes.setup: The power has been cut at the party, and Leslie and Tom have been in the hot tub having an emotional conversation.
jokes.punchline: Tom's reason for staying in the hot tub — equal parts sadness and pruning — is a perfectly Tom combination of emotional and aesthetic concerns.
jokes.explanation: A gem of a line. 'I'm too sad to get out, and I'm all pruney' perfectly captures Tom's character — even in genuine emotional distress, he's tracking his physical appearance. The listing of 'sadness' and 'pruning' as equivalent reasons with the word 'and' is the structural key. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Tom explaining Entertainment 720's bankruptcy: 'They say you've got to spend money to make money. Well, I don't know where we went wrong. We spent all of our money.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains that Entertainment 720 has been hemorrhaging cash.
jokes.punchline: He invokes the 'spend money to make money' principle as his business philosophy, then reveals with genuine confusion that they followed it perfectly — they spent all the money — but somehow it didn't work.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is perfectly constructed — Tom has taken a cliché business saying (spend money to make money) and followed only the first half with perfect faithfulness, apparently unable to understand why the second half didn't materialize automatically. 'I don't know where we went wrong. We spent all of our money.' is delivered with genuine bewilderment. The economy is superb — this is a complete diagnosis of Tom's business failure in two sentences. Highly quotable and a perfect capsule of the character's fundamental flaw.

jokes.text: Leslie suggesting 'comfort food' and Tom asking for 'albacore tuna with crispy onions' as comfort food
jokes.setup: Leslie offers Tom comfort food as a way to cheer him up after the bankruptcy revelation.
jokes.punchline: When Tom names his comfort food — 'albacore tuna with crispy onions at this hour?' — it's both specific and upscale, the opposite of conventional comfort food (mac and cheese, etc.). It's exactly Tom.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. Tom's comfort food being an upscale fish dish is perfectly in character — even in sadness, he maintains his refined (or self-imagined refined) taste. 'At this hour?' adds to the specificity.

jokes.text: Andy says 'the flange was a little warped, so I just goosed it with a triple-three bolt smack.' Ron: 'That was nonsense.' Andy: 'I know, but it's so fun to talk like that.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been teaching Andy home repair; Andy has been absorbing technical vocabulary
jokes.punchline: Andy has been using completely made-up technical jargon for the joy of sounding knowledgeable; Ron calls him out and Andy immediately agrees it's nonsense but defends it as fun
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Andy's motivations are always immediate and joy-based, and discovering that technical jargon is fun to say without meaning anything is completely Andy. 'I know, but it's so fun to talk like that' is the perfect admission — transparent self-justification. The fake technical phrase 'goosed it with a triple-three bolt smack' is great writing in itself. Ron's flat 'That was nonsense' before Andy's admission is perfectly structured.

jokes.text: Ron and April's fake plumbing talk: 'I'd say you've got the handle on that torque wrench.' / 'Yeah, well, the flange was a little warped, so I just goosed it with a triple-three bolt smack.' / 'That was nonsense.' / 'I know, but it's so fun to talk like that.'
jokes.setup: Ron and April are bonding over fixing the house. April mimics Ron's confident plumbing talk.
jokes.punchline: April invents fake plumbing jargon ('triple-three bolt smack'), Ron immediately calls it nonsense, and April confirms she knows but finds it fun. Ron's deadpan reaction to the nonsense is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character exchange. The joke works on multiple levels: April attempting Ron's register, the specific invented jargon ('triple-three bolt smack' is a great fake phrase), Ron's immediate and certain identification of nonsense ('That was nonsense'), and April's cheerful admission. It's also a beautiful Ron/April bonding moment — he doesn't mock her for it, just confirms the fact. 'I know, but it's so fun to talk like that' is a gem of a line. Their relationship is one of the show's best, and this exchange is a microcosm of why.

jokes.text: Ron giving April his toolbox and saying 'You earned it.'
jokes.setup: Ron has bonded with April over fixing the house. He gives her his personal toolbox.
jokes.punchline: Ron giving someone his tools is played completely seriously as a meaningful gift — and IT IS meaningful for Ron — but presented without sentimentality ('You earned it'). The comedy is in the restraint.
jokes.explanation: A sweet Ron moment with comedic underpinning. For Ron, giving someone his toolbox is a profound act of trust and respect. 'You earned it' delivered with total deadpan seriousness is funny because of how disproportionately significant this is in Ron's value system — you'd expect this level of gravitas for saving a life, not for helping fix a faucet.

jokes.text: Blood capsule reveal: 'Psych! Blood capsules... I wanted to shock you into expressing your anger.' / 'My nose is broken.'
jokes.setup: Ben appears to have been hurt in the wrestling match — blood everywhere. Andy looks horrified.
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals it was the fake blood capsules from the opening, used as a therapy tool. Then Ben clarifies that his nose IS actually broken.
jokes.explanation: A triumphant callback to the opening. The blood capsules mentioned in the first minute pay off here in a double-twist: (1) the blood is fake — it's the capsules from the shopping list, and (2) the nose IS actually broken anyway. The structure is excellent — double misdirection. The callback rewards attentive viewers while the 'my nose is broken' button lands as a dark, funny conclusion. This is the episode's best structural joke in terms of long-form construction.

jokes.text: Leslie pointing out that Tom turned people away for the first two weeks by claiming to be booked: 'Kind of seems like regular sight should have caught that one.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains that E 720 told everyone they were booked solid for the first two weeks as a demand-creation strategy. Leslie says '20/20 hindsight.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response to Tom's 'hindsight is 20/20' is that this was so obviously stupid that normal, non-hindsight vision should have caught it.
jokes.explanation: A sharp comeback that subverts the 'hindsight is 20/20' cliché. Tom's use of the phrase implies his mistake was forgivable and only visible in retrospect; Leslie's response denies him even that comfort, arguing it was obvious in real time. The logic is airtight and the delivery is quick. High quotability.

jokes.text: Leslie's backhanded compliment to Tom: 'You're a smart guy and charming occasionally.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to encourage Tom after his company's bankruptcy.
jokes.punchline: 'Charming occasionally' — even in a sincere pep talk, Leslie can't help qualifying Tom's charm as intermittent.
jokes.explanation: A nice understated joke. The 'occasionally' qualifier undercuts what's supposed to be a heartfelt encouragement without being cruel. It's Leslie being honest when she's trying to be kind, which is very Leslie.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Also, your logo, it's the worst logo I've ever seen. It doesn't make any sense. It's gibberish.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is cataloguing E720's business failures; they're in the hot tub together
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots from strategic critique to aesthetic critique — the logo is apparently so bad it's 'gibberish'
jokes.explanation: The word 'gibberish' is doing the most work here — it implies the logo transcends bad design into incoherence. Works as a punctuating joke in the critique sequence.

jokes.text: Ben's list of reasonable grievances ends with: 'Stop using my comforter for your pillow forts.'
jokes.setup: Ben is finally expressing his grievances about living with Andy and April — things like respecting his space and telling him about events.
jokes.punchline: Among the legitimate adult concerns, 'stop using my comforter for your pillow forts' is both specific and revealing — Andy and April are building pillow forts in the common area using Ben's bedding.
jokes.explanation: A specific, funny detail. Pillow forts as an established activity for April and Andy adds to their characterization as grown children. The specificity of 'my comforter' is what makes it land — it's not a generic complaint but a very particular violation.

jokes.text: Andy's counter-demand: pay for studio recording time for his band, 'about 5,600 bucks. Deal?'
jokes.setup: Ben has expressed his grievances and Andy says 'Absolutely. Really? Yep.' — seemingly agreeing unconditionally.
jokes.punchline: Andy adds one condition: Ben pays $5,600 for studio recording time. The number is very specific and very large — a complete non-sequitur to the roommate conflict.
jokes.explanation: Good Andy joke. The 'one thing' being a specific dollar amount for an unrelated expense reveals Andy's childlike transactional thinking. '$5,600' being very specific (not 'about $5,000' or 'a few thousand') suggests Andy has actually looked this up, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Hospital scene: 'You his friend?' / 'Him? Hell, no. We're brothers.'
jokes.setup: At the hospital after Ben's broken nose, a nurse/staff member asks April if Ben is her friend.
jokes.punchline: 'Hell, no. We're brothers.' — April denies friendship while claiming a deeper (and biologically impossible) bond. She won't call Ben her friend but claims brotherhood.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character moment and emotional payoff disguised as a joke. April can't admit affection for Ben directly, so she expresses it by denying friendship (too weak) and claiming brotherhood (stronger, weirder). The 'Hell, no' vehemence followed immediately by the deeper claim is perfectly April. It's also the emotional resolution of the entire Ben/April subplot. Very quotable, deeply character-specific — only April would express care through aggressive denial.

jokes.text: April: 'Ew. If your nose is all weird after this, I'm totally going to divorce you.' / Andy: 'Whatever. I'm going to divorce you first for wearing my favorite hoodie.'
jokes.setup: At the hospital, April is looking at Andy's potentially broken nose.
jokes.punchline: The marital threat ('I'm going to divorce you') escalates to a counter-threat, and Andy's reason for divorce is that April is wearing his hoodie — a trivially petty grievance elevated to divorce-worthy status.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful April/Andy joke that reveals their relationship. They threaten divorce the way others would threaten mild inconvenience, and Andy's counter-divorce-threat being about a hoodie is perfectly calibrated. The implication is that these two would divorce and immediately get back together over nothing — which is very them. 'I'm going to divorce you first' is great competitive framing.

jokes.text: Ben's final exit: April tells Andy they can't use Ben's comforter anymore. Andy: 'What are we going to have sex on?'
jokes.setup: The conflict with Ben has been resolved. April reports the one condition: no more comforter for pillow forts.
jokes.punchline: Andy's question reveals that the comforter apparently serves double duty in ways Ben doesn't know about.
jokes.explanation: A good callback button. The joke recontextualizes the comforter dispute by implying it's been used for more than pillow forts — and Ben doesn't know. Andy's genuine confusion about alternative options is funny. Solid episode-closing joke for this subplot.

jokes.text: Tom's video biography of Leslie opening: 'The year was 1975. It was a time of trouble. Watergate. Well, I'm not a crook. Vietnam. Peter Gabriel leaves Genesis.'
jokes.setup: Tom has made Leslie a video biography to make up for the campaign event disaster.
jokes.punchline: The historical context Tom invokes for Leslie's birth includes Watergate and Vietnam — then 'Peter Gabriel leaves Genesis' as an equivalent world-historical crisis.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The escalating historical catastrophes — Watergate, Vietnam — set up a grave tone, then 'Peter Gabriel leaves Genesis' treats a rock-band lineup change as equivalent world history. It also reveals something about Tom: he genuinely cares about this as history. The inclusion of the Nixon voice ('Well, I'm not a crook') as a quoted source is also a funny detail. The joke works perfectly as an absurdist escalation and as character comedy (Tom's worldview includes Genesis breakups as civilizational events).

jokes.text: Tom's description of himself in Leslie's video: 'Tom Haverford is a selfish, unctuous, sleazy, self-promoting, good-hearted, secretly kind and wonderful, tiny little person.'
jokes.setup: Tom is narrating a video biography of Leslie and pivots to describing himself.
jokes.punchline: The list of adjectives begins with accurate negatives (selfish, unctuous, sleazy, self-promoting) and then pivots to sincere positives — all delivered with the same serious-documentary voice — before ending with 'tiny little person.'
jokes.explanation: Superb character comedy and the emotional core of the Tom subplot. The joke works on three levels: (1) the comic contrast between the negative and positive adjectives, (2) the revelation that Tom sees himself clearly and still likes himself, and (3) 'tiny little person' as the completely deflating button after all the grandeur. It's also genuinely touching — Tom inserting himself into Leslie's bio as a form of tribute and self-assessment. 'Unctuous' is a delightfully specific word for Tom to use about himself.

jokes.text: Tom's video invoking Li'l Sebastian: 'And if Li'l Sebastian were still alive, he'd surely vote for her.'
jokes.setup: Tom's video biography of Leslie is building to a sincere endorsement.
jokes.punchline: Tom invokes the memory of Li'l Sebastian — the beloved miniature horse who died — as a hypothetical endorser. This is both a Parks and Rec inside reference and a genuine emotional beat.
jokes.explanation: A great series callback. Li'l Sebastian's death was one of the show's biggest emotional moments, and invoking him here as a hypothetical endorser is both funny and touching. The 'surely' is a nice word — as if Tom has consulted Sebastian's known political views. High impact for fans of the show.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to Tom's video: 'I'm going to watch it every day for the rest of my life. And when I die, I'm going to project it on my tombstone.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks if Leslie liked his video biography.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's expression of enthusiasm escalates from daily viewing to posthumous tombstone projection — a completely sincere Leslie statement that is also absurd.
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie enthusiasm joke. She means every word completely sincerely, which is what makes it funny. The tombstone escalation is the right ending — Leslie would 100% request this. 'Project it on my tombstone' is a very specific and funny technological vision of afterlife vanity.

jokes.text: Chris's talking head: '...the culprit was Millicent Gergich.' / 'You should look into actual detective work.' / 'I will.'
jokes.setup: Chris (Sherlock Holmes costume) gives a dramatic talking-head about having 'an amazing time at that party' and reveals who 'stole his heart.'
jokes.punchline: He delivers the revelation in Sherlock Holmes detective mode ('the culprit was Millicent Gergich'), then takes Ben's sarcastic suggestion about detective work completely literally and enthusiastically.
jokes.explanation: Good Chris joke. 'The culprit was Millicent Gergich' is a wonderful delivery — Chris has stayed in Sherlock Holmes mode for what is apparently a sincere romantic announcement. Ben's sarcasm going completely over Chris's head ('I will') is textbook Chris Traeger — his literalist positivity is unstoppable.

jokes.text: Chris to Jerry about his daughter: 'I've decided to take your daughter home. And we may be having intercourse.' / Jerry: 'Please, you've got to stop saying things like that to me.'
jokes.setup: Chris is wrapping up the party and addressing Jerry, his date's father.
jokes.punchline: Chris's radical honesty and total social tone-deafness leads him to announce potential sexual activity with Jerry's daughter directly to Jerry, framed in the clinical language of someone who believes in transparency.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best cringe jokes. 'We may be having intercourse' said to the father with complete sincerity and positivity is textbook Chris Traeger — his commitment to honesty and positivity overrides all social convention. Jerry's 'you've got to stop saying things like that to me' implies this is a recurring situation, which makes it even better. 'Intercourse' as the specific word choice (clinical, not casual) is perfect.

jokes.text: Final tag: Ben can't find his car keys. April: 'Solve this mystery, genius.' — referring to Ben's Sherlock Holmes-less evening
jokes.setup: Ben says he can't find his car keys. April responds.
jokes.punchline: 'Solve this mystery, genius' — a callback to Chris's Sherlock Holmes costume and the detective theme of the evening, now directed sarcastically at a non-costumed, non-detective Ben.
jokes.explanation: A solid episode-closing joke. April's sarcastic use of 'genius' and 'solve this mystery' ties back to the Sherlock Holmes thread while also being a good April insult. Economical and ends the episode on the right note — April and Ben's relationship has progressed but she still won't stop ribbing him.

tmdb_overview: Andy and April host a Halloween bash at their house. Tom emcees an event for Leslie's campaign. Andy and April receive an unusual wedding present from Ron and Ann.
insight: Character comedy carries a narrowly-missed top-tier episode with 34 jokes in 49 minutes.
